column1: What is the primary objective of an audit of financial statements?
column2: To enable the auditor to express an opinion on whether the FS give a true and fair view (are free from material misstatement) — assurance, not certification of absolute accuracy.

column1: Why can an audit give only reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance?
column2: Inherent limitations: use of judgement/estimates, test-checking (sampling), persuasive-not-conclusive evidence, management fraud/collusion, and nature of items — 100% certainty is impossible and uneconomical.

column1: What is the difference between reasonable assurance and absolute assurance?
column2: Reasonable = high but not 100% (audit); absolute = 100% guarantee (never given). Auditor reduces risk to acceptably low, not zero.

column1: Why is an auditor a 'watchdog and not a bloodhound' (Kingston Cotton Mills)?
column2: He must exercise reasonable care/skill and is entitled to rely on trusted officials unless something arouses suspicion — not bound to approach work with pre-set suspicion of fraud.

column1: What are the two pillars/objectives of audit under SA 200?
column2: (1) Obtain reasonable assurance FS are free from material misstatement; (2) Report on the FS and communicate as required by the SAs.

column1: What is 'true and fair view' — why not 'true and correct'?
column2: Accounts need not be arithmetically exact; they must reflect economic reality free of material misstatement and comply with the applicable framework — fairness over pin-point correctness.

column1: Define audit materiality (SA 320).
column2: Misstatements are material if they, individually or aggregated, could reasonably be expected to influence economic decisions of users taken on the basis of the FS.

column1: Why is materiality a matter of professional judgement, not a fixed percentage?
column2: It depends on size AND nature of the item and the surrounding circumstances; qualitative factors (e.g. fraud, compliance) can make a small amount material.

column1: What is performance materiality and why set it below overall materiality?
column2: Amount set below overall materiality to reduce the risk that aggregate of uncorrected + undetected misstatements exceeds materiality — a buffer for undetected errors.

column1: State the audit risk model.
column2: Audit Risk = Risk of Material Misstatement × Detection Risk = (Inherent Risk × Control Risk) × Detection Risk.

column1: Why does detection risk vary inversely with risk of material misstatement?
column2: To keep audit risk acceptably low: when RMM is high, auditor must lower detection risk by doing more/better substantive work; when RMM is low, DR can be higher.

column1: What is inherent risk?
column2: Susceptibility of an assertion to misstatement (before controls), due to complexity, estimation, or nature of the item — e.g. cash and estimates carry high inherent risk.

column1: What is control risk?
column2: Risk that a misstatement will not be prevented or detected and corrected on a timely basis by the entity's internal control.

column1: What is detection risk?
column2: Risk that the auditor's procedures will not detect an existing material misstatement — the only component the auditor directly controls.

column1: Why must an auditor maintain professional scepticism (SA 200)?
column2: A questioning mind alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement and critical assessment of evidence — guards against over-reliance on management and undue trust.

column1: What is professional judgement in auditing?
column2: Application of relevant training, knowledge and experience in making informed decisions about courses of action appropriate in the audit circumstances.

column1: Why is documentation (SA 230) essential — 'not done if not documented'?
column2: Provides evidence of the basis for the opinion and that the audit complied with SAs; supports planning, review, quality control, and defence in litigation.

column1: What is the SA 230 rule for assembling the final audit file?
column2: Assemble on a timely basis, ordinarily within 60 days of the auditor's report date; retain for at least 7 years (SQC 1).

column1: Define audit evidence and its two quality attributes (SA 500).
column2: Information used to draw conclusions supporting the opinion; must be sufficient (quantity) and appropriate (relevance + reliability).

column1: Why is externally sourced/original evidence more reliable?
column2: Reliability rises with independence of source, effective internal control, direct auditor knowledge, documentary form, and originals over copies — external confirmations rank high.

column1: What is the difference between 'sufficient' and 'appropriate' evidence?
column2: Sufficient = enough quantity (affected by risk & quality); Appropriate = quality — relevant to the assertion and reliable. Higher risk/lower quality needs more quantity.

column1: List the financial statement assertions about transactions.
column2: Occurrence, Completeness, Accuracy, Cut-off, Classification (and Presentation).

column1: List the assertions about account balances at period end.
column2: Existence, Rights & Obligations, Completeness, Valuation & Allocation (Accuracy, Classification, Presentation).

column1: Why test 'existence' for assets but 'completeness' for liabilities?
column2: Management tends to overstate assets (test they exist) and understate liabilities (test all are recorded) — audit direction follows the likely misstatement.

column1: What is vouching?
column2: Examination of documentary evidence to verify the authenticity, authority and accuracy of a recorded transaction — tests occurrence/validity of entries.

column1: What is verification?
column2: Examining assets and liabilities for existence, ownership, valuation and presentation at the B/S date — confirms the balance, not just the transaction.

column1: Difference between vouching and verification.
column2: Vouching checks entries in books (transactions during the year); verification checks assets/liabilities existence and value at period end. Vouching precedes verification.

column1: What is the auditor's duty regarding valuation of assets — does he value them?
column2: No. Valuation is management's responsibility; the auditor verifies the reasonableness of the values and disclosures, exercising due care.

column1: Why is closing stock valued at lower of cost or NRV (AS 2)?
column2: Prudence — never carry an asset above its realisable cash; recognise the probable loss now but never an unrealised gain.

column1: What are the two error types in audit sampling (SA 530)?
column2: Sampling risk (sample not representative) and non-sampling risk (auditor error — wrong procedure, misinterpretation), the latter reduced by planning/supervision.

column1: What is the difference between statistical and non-statistical sampling?
column2: Statistical uses random selection + probability theory to measure sampling risk; non-statistical relies on judgement and cannot quantify sampling risk.

column1: What is the going concern assumption (SA 570)?
column2: FS are prepared on the basis that the entity will continue operations for the foreseeable future and has no need/intention to liquidate — else break-up basis is used.

column1: What does the auditor do if a material uncertainty on going concern is adequately disclosed?
column2: Express an unmodified opinion and add a separate 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern' paragraph drawing attention to the note.

column1: Define fraud vs error (SA 240).
column2: Fraud = intentional act to obtain unjust/illegal advantage; Error = unintentional mistake. The distinguishing factor is intent.

column1: What are the two types of fraud under SA 240?
column2: Fraudulent financial reporting (misstating FS) and misappropriation of assets (theft).

column1: Whose responsibility is prevention and detection of fraud?
column2: Primarily those charged with governance and management (via internal control); the auditor is responsible only for reasonable assurance FS are free of material misstatement.

column1: When must an auditor report fraud to the Central Government (Sec 143(12))?
column2: When fraud against the company by officers/employees involves amount of Rs 1 crore or more — report to CG (via Form ADT-4) within prescribed time.

column1: What is done for fraud below Rs 1 crore under Sec 143(12)?
column2: Report to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days; company discloses details in the Board's Report.

column1: What is the purpose of Standards on Auditing (SAs)?
column2: Mandatory professional standards prescribing principles/procedures the auditor must follow; non-compliance requires disclosure and can attract disciplinary action.

column1: SA 210 covers what?
column2: Agreeing the terms of audit engagements — the engagement letter documenting scope, responsibilities of management and auditor, and reporting framework.

column1: Why is an engagement letter (SA 210) important?
column2: Confirms acceptance, avoids misunderstanding on scope/responsibilities, and evidences the auditor–client contract; management acknowledges its responsibilities.

column1: SA 220 deals with what?
column2: Quality control for an audit of financial statements — engagement partner's responsibility for direction, supervision, review and consultation.

column1: SA 260 requires communication with whom, about what?
column2: Those charged with governance — planned scope/timing, significant findings, auditor independence, and significant difficulties encountered.

column1: SA 265 deals with what?
column2: Communicating deficiencies in internal control to those charged with governance and management — significant deficiencies in writing.

column1: SA 299 deals with what?
column2: Responsibility of joint auditors — division of work, coordination, and each joint auditor being responsible for their allotted area yet jointly for common areas.

column1: SA 315 deals with what?
column2: Identifying and assessing risks of material misstatement through understanding the entity and its environment, including internal control.

column1: SA 330 deals with what?
column2: The auditor's responses to assessed risks — designing tests of controls and substantive procedures to address RMM.

column1: SA 402 deals with what?
column2: Audit considerations relating to an entity using a service organisation (e.g. outsourced payroll) and Type 1/Type 2 reports.

column1: SA 450 deals with what?
column2: Evaluation of misstatements identified during the audit — accumulating, communicating for correction, and assessing effect on the opinion.

column1: SA 500 vs SA 501 — the difference?
column2: SA 500 = audit evidence generally; SA 501 = specific considerations for selected items (inventory attendance, litigation/claims, segment information).

column1: SA 505 covers what?
column2: External confirmations — direct written responses from third parties (e.g. bank, debtors) obtained by the auditor; positive vs negative confirmation.

column1: SA 510 deals with what?
column2: Initial audit engagements — opening balances; ensuring opening balances are free of misstatement and consistent policies applied.

column1: SA 520 deals with what?
column2: Analytical procedures — evaluations of financial data through plausible relationships (ratios, trends), used at planning and overall review stages.

column1: SA 550 deals with what?
column2: Related parties — identifying and disclosing related party relationships and transactions and assessing associated risks.

column1: SA 560 deals with what?
column2: Subsequent events — events between B/S date and the auditor's report date (and facts discovered after), adjusting vs non-adjusting.

column1: SA 580 deals with what?
column2: Written representations — statements by management confirming responsibilities and specific assertions; supplement, not substitute for, other evidence.

column1: SA 600 deals with what?
column2: Using the work of another auditor (branch/component); principal auditor's responsibility and reliance on the other auditor.

column1: SA 610 vs SA 620 — the difference?
column2: SA 610 = using the work of internal auditors; SA 620 = using the work of an auditor's expert (valuer, actuary, engineer).

column1: What are the types of audit opinion (SA 700/705)?
column2: Unmodified (clean) and three modified: Qualified, Adverse, Disclaimer of opinion.

column1: When is a Qualified opinion given?
column2: Misstatements are material but NOT pervasive, OR unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence but possible effects are material but not pervasive — 'except for'.

column1: When is an Adverse opinion given?
column2: Misstatements are BOTH material AND pervasive — FS as a whole do not give a true and fair view.

column1: When is a Disclaimer of opinion given?
column2: Auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and possible effects are BOTH material AND pervasive — cannot form an opinion.

column1: What does 'pervasive' mean in the opinion decision (SA 705)?
column2: Effects not confined to specific elements — either widespread through the FS, or if confined, represent a substantial proportion, or are fundamental to users' understanding.

column1: What is an Emphasis of Matter paragraph (SA 706)?
column2: Draws attention to a matter properly presented/disclosed in the FS that is fundamental to users' understanding — does NOT modify the opinion.

column1: Emphasis of Matter vs Other Matter paragraph.
column2: EOM refers to a matter presented/disclosed IN the FS; Other Matter refers to a matter NOT presented in the FS but relevant to users' understanding of the audit/report.

column1: What are Key Audit Matters (SA 701)?
column2: Matters that, in the auditor's professional judgement, were of most significance in the audit — mandatory for listed entities; not a substitute for an opinion.

column1: Who is eligible to be a company auditor (Sec 141)?
column2: A Chartered Accountant in practice; a firm/LLP where majority of partners practising in India are qualified may be appointed in the firm's name.

column1: Name two grounds of disqualification of an auditor under Sec 141(3).
column2: Body corporate (except LLP), officer/employee of the company, holding security/interest in the company, or indebtedness exceeding Rs 5 lakh.

column1: What is the ceiling on number of audits per person (Sec 141(3)(g))?
column2: Maximum 20 companies per person (excluding OPCs, dormant, small and private companies with paid-up capital < Rs 100 crore).

column1: How is the first auditor of a company appointed (Sec 139(6))?
column2: By the Board within 30 days of registration; if Board fails, by members in EGM within 90 days; holds office till conclusion of the 1st AGM.

column1: What is the term of a subsequent auditor (Sec 139(1))?
column2: Appointed at AGM to hold office from that AGM till the conclusion of the 6th AGM (subject to ratification rules), i.e. a 5-year term.

column1: What is auditor rotation under Sec 139(2)?
column2: Listed & prescribed companies: individual auditor max 1 term of 5 years; firm max 2 terms of 5 years — then a 5-year cooling-off period.

column1: How can an auditor be removed before term expiry (Sec 140(1))?
column2: Special resolution + prior approval of the Central Government (via Form ADT-2), after giving the auditor a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

column1: What must a resigning auditor file (Sec 140(2))?
column2: Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar (and CAG if applicable) within 30 days of resignation, stating reasons.

column1: What are the auditor's powers under Sec 143(1)?
column2: Right of access at all times to books, accounts and vouchers, and to require information/explanations necessary for the audit.

column1: What is the auditor's basic duty under Sec 143?
column2: To make a report to members on the accounts examined and on every FS, stating whether they give a true and fair view and comply with the Act/standards.

column1: What is CARO 2020?
column2: Companies (Auditor's Report) Order — additional reporting matters (21 clauses) the auditor must comment on, e.g. fixed assets, inventory, loans, statutory dues, fraud.

column1: What is reporting on Internal Financial Controls (Sec 143(3)(i))?
column2: Auditor must state whether the company has adequate IFC over financial reporting and their operating effectiveness — for prescribed companies.

column1: Define Internal Control (SA 315).
column2: Process designed by governance/management to provide reasonable assurance on reliability of reporting, effectiveness/efficiency of operations, and compliance with laws.

column1: What are the inherent limitations of internal control?
column2: Human error, management override, collusion, cost-benefit constraints, and controls becoming inadequate due to changed conditions — hence only reasonable assurance.

column1: What is a walk-through test?
column2: Tracing one/few transactions through the entire accounting system to confirm the auditor's understanding of the design and implementation of controls.

column1: What is the difference between tests of controls and substantive procedures?
column2: Tests of controls check whether controls operate effectively; substantive procedures detect material misstatements at the assertion level (details + analytics).

column1: What is an internal check?
column2: Arrangement of duties so that no single person handles a transaction end-to-end; work of one is automatically checked by another — a fraud-prevention design.

column1: Why must audit of a Not-for-Profit / charitable institution focus on receipts?
column2: Income is often unrecorded/cash-based (donations, subscriptions); the key risk is completeness of receipts, so the auditor stresses income controls.

column1: What is the Chartered Accountants Act framework for professional ethics?
column2: Two Schedules; First & Second Schedules list acts of professional/other misconduct — Second covers graver misconduct with heavier penalties.

column1: What is 'professional misconduct' — the two branches of the CA Act schedules?
column2: First Schedule (less grave, e.g. sharing fees, advertising) and Second Schedule (grave, e.g. gross negligence, disclosing client info) misconduct.

column1: What are the five fundamental principles of the Code of Ethics?
column2: Integrity, Objectivity, Professional Competence & Due Care, Confidentiality, and Professional Behaviour.

column1: What is the difference between independence of mind and independence in appearance?
column2: Mind = state permitting an unbiased opinion free of influences; Appearance = avoiding facts/circumstances a reasonable third party would see as compromising integrity/objectivity.

column1: Name the five threats to independence in the Code of Ethics.
column2: Self-interest, Self-review, Advocacy, Familiarity, and Intimidation threats.

column1: Give an example of a self-review threat.
column2: Auditor evaluating results of a previous judgement/service they performed (e.g. having prepared the accounting records now being audited).

column1: Why is an auditor prohibited from a contingent fee based on findings?
column2: It creates a self-interest threat that impairs objectivity and independence — the fee should not depend on the audit outcome.

column1: What is the difference between an audit and an investigation?
column2: Audit forms an opinion on true and fair view for a period; investigation is a special, in-depth probe for a specific purpose (fraud, acquisition), often beyond one year.

column1: What is a management representation letter's evidential value?
column2: It is corroborative evidence; where other sufficient appropriate evidence is expected to exist, a representation alone is not enough and cannot replace it.

column1: What is the auditor's responsibility for comparatives / prior period figures (SA 710)?
column2: To obtain evidence that comparatives are free of material misstatement and consistently classified; corresponding figures are covered by the current opinion.

column1: What is 'test checking'?
column2: Examining a representative sample rather than 100% of transactions, based on the reliability of internal control — an application of sampling to gain efficiency.

column1: Why is cut-off procedure important at the year-end?
column2: To ensure transactions are recorded in the correct accounting period (occurrence/completeness) — misclassifying near year-end distorts profit and balances.

column1: What is the difference between a compliance audit and a substantive audit approach?
column2: Compliance (controls) approach relies on effective internal controls to reduce substantive testing; substantive approach tests transactions/balances directly when controls are weak.

column1: What is the auditor's duty if the FS omit a required disclosure?
column2: Discuss with management; if not corrected and material, include the information in the report if practicable and modify the opinion (qualified/adverse).
